QUIBBLE.name: Bill
QUIBBLE.direction: Old pompous pirate captain, gravelly theatrical boasts.

FINE PRINT.name: Charlie
FINE PRINT.direction: Quick, mischievous parrot, bright emphatic comic delivery.

NELL.name: Alice
NELL.direction: Clear, lively young adventurer; curious and dryly amused.

MARA.name: Matilda
MARA.direction: Warm, grounded tavern keeper; measured delivery and dry humour.

ORIN.name: Bill
ORIN.direction: Low, seasoned older navigator; unhurried storyteller.

records.text: Who actually saw the current change?
The ferry clerk saw her loose line turn. The fish seller saw the launch. The lantern tender heard two bells. None saw a ghost, which has inconvenienced my layout.
Two bells?
One outside, one from the old return pipe. I called it an answer.
To what question?
That was going to be tomorrow's edition.
Your headline says the lighthouse predicts yesterday.
An exclusive.
Yesterday is unusually well covered.
Yes. Competition has been brutal.
Do you know the name Rook?
Town lane, house with the weather vane that argues with the wind. Dr. Rook builds mechanisms. Her family built reasons not to discuss them.
Orin's ship is missing.
Then I owe him a correction. I printed that it had retired.
Did anyone see it?
A striped cabin behind the old yard screen. The witness could not see a name.
Will you print what I find?
If I can show readers how you know it.
Even if it's less exciting?
I have a very large typeface. I can make accuracy look alarming.
I need tracing paper.
The clean tray. Same public supply as the quay. Please don't take a headline; they're still wet.
Back to the harbour.
Bring facts. I can provide the exclamation marks.
What is breakfast waiting for?
The heater waits for the serving bell. The bell waits for the table. The table waits for the heater to finish. My grandfather called this perfect supervision.
Why not turn the whole thing off?
The trolley brake releases under local control. Kill the supply and it stays across the workshop door, celebrating its final decision.
Could each part do its own job?
Yes. The labels explain how. I have been rather busy preventing the tea from entering a new state of matter.
Can I help?
Keep the heater warm, park the table, put the bell on hand control. Then release the trolley. In that order, if you value the cups.
Does the harbour work like your breakfast?
Not literally. I have never charged a ship for marmalade. Finish here and I will show you the distinction.
I'll look at the controls.
Read the little words. My family spent generations engraving them and minutes following them.
Is this your relay?
Our pattern, replacement shutters. This number belongs to the repair-yard service inlet. Here is its drawing.
Bring a maker's name and relay number. The retired housing on the quay should still have its plate.
Why did nobody mention the service channel?
It was for inspections, not through traffic. Commercial charts stopped printing it. Water is less attentive to revised editions.
How do I inspect the barrier safely?
Set the inlet to INSPECT. Open the equalising valve. Wait for the two marked levels to agree. Then turn the local crank. The interlock prevents you doing the dangerous version.
Can I borrow that crank?
Yes. It only fits this inspection socket. Please return it to its bracket when the barrier is latched.
Let me identify the mechanism first. ‘Approximately the right crank’ is a dangerous engineering tradition.
Can a local station disagree with the central controls?
For inspection, yes. Larger coordination is another matter. This drawing covers one barrier, not the whole network.
Why are you reluctant to discuss your family?
We put our name on systems before we understood everyone who would depend on them.
And now?
Now I read the little words.
Vane offered to pay for my measurements.
Accurate measurements are useful. Ask what permission travels with them.
Could she use them to make it safer?
Yes. That is why the question matters.
I freed the ship.
Then the inspection route did its job. Leave the barrier in its marked safe position.
I should get back to the quay.
If a mechanism surprises you, stop turning it. An unpopular but serviceable rule.
I'm following the signal equipment.
Then find who made it, who uses it, and who says those are the same person.
I borrowed your boathook.
Bring it back when it has finished being useful. It was wasted on the wall.
Vane says my work is worth paying for.
It is. That doesn't tell you what she wants to buy.
Should I take the commission?
Read it. Keep your original. Ask what happens to the copy. The choice is yours.
I found Orin's ship.
Good. Perhaps he'll stop using my tables to demonstrate where it isn't.
Do you know anything about the old gates?
Enough to know their drawings deserve care. Bring me what you can actually establish.
I'll keep looking.
Eat something before you decide the fate of the harbour.
Why didn't you look behind the screen?
The notice said CLOSED CHANNEL. I interpreted it rather completely.
I saw the stripes and the kettle.
Then she is there.
You sound surprised.
Relieved. I have been performing surprise to avoid that.
Come to the inlet.
Open the inspection access safely first. I can wait without making another navigational decision.
I'll meet you there. Bring a proper mooring line.
Any advice on the old survey?
Trust fixed marks. Correct what you can measure. Leave a clear note where you can't.
I'm investigating the company's trials.
At last. A rival with enough paperwork to deserve being called a trial.
Record dates. Insults age poorly as evidence.
What does ‘operational use of measurements’ mean?
It means they may operate using the measurements. A sentence can be perfectly honest and still deserve your attention.
Their licence allows public inspection.
Then inspect publicly.
Safely. He omits adverbs when excited.
I found a way to recover Orin's ship.
A fine rescue. I once rescued a fleet.
Of receipts. From a puddle.
I need advice, not another duel.
Then you may cross. I am experimenting with relevance.
What will you do with my copy?
Calibrate the service route and coordinate it with our marked passage. The commission says operational use.
Will other boats benefit?
A dependable harbour benefits every operator. The terms of access will be published.
That is not the same as free access.
No. Maintenance, crews and liability cost money. I do not propose to finance them with optimism.
My evidence doesn't prove you caused every change.
Correct. That distinction is one reason I am hiring you.
The trials hid Orin's ship.
His vessel followed a trial marker into a service basin. We will correct the notice. I am paying for better measurements because imperfect arrangements have consequences.
I want public safety written into the purpose.
Agreed: ‘for safe local routing.’ The operating-policy clause remains.
I would like the credit to say independent surveyor.
Independent surveyor Nell. A precise description.
I need time to decide.
Take it. Precision is wasted if you sign without reading.
You knew what I wanted this to achieve.
I knew you wanted accurate routes and paid work. You have provided the first and received the second.
Safety doesn't require owning every way through.
Someone must accept responsibility for coordinating them.
Responsibility isn't the same as exclusive permission.
We disagree about the practical difference.
Withdraw my name.
I can record your objection. I cannot pretend the work was not yours.
Can we leave now?
She is ready. Finish your business ashore and speak to Mara. I will check the rigging; no voyage improves because someone skipped that.
Do you mind if I question your route?
I have named the ship Second Opinion. It would be poor seamanship to object.
What did we prove?
That the new marker diverted me, and a barrier hid the vessel. Not who gave the order. Keep those separate.
What do you make of the company announcement?
Your name is on their route sheet.
So is the measurement I gave them.
Then we print the distinction. A correction is not an erasure.
I told you to ask about permission.
I asked. I wanted the answer to mean something kinder.
Then next time we must make the answer less optional.
Compulsory contracts. The word ‘all’ has found its teeth.
Can we stop it?
Not by cutting something we don't understand.
The boat is ready.
I have something to put right before we sail.
Then start with the person you need to tell.
You look as though being right has gone badly.
I need to tell you what I gave Vane.
Then we'll make time.
Nell? Your drawing distinguishes a current from a rumour. That is rarer than you might think.
You read my notes?
The public account. I would like to pay for a more complete survey.
Of the channel, or of how much I know?
The first. The second appears to be increasing without my assistance.
Bring measurements, Miss Nell. I have cupboards full of assurances.
For once, a qualification I possess.
Welcome to the Quay Quill. Are you news, a correction, or here about the roof?
The water changed direction after a company signal.
News. Possibly a correction to several things I printed about the water.
Can I see the original reports?
Certainly. The facts are underneath the adjectives.
Signal, current, launch. Three facts in order. I've had shorter careers in journalism.
I compared the reports at the quay.
Excellent. I shall describe this as our distributed newsroom.
I'll change ‘predicts’ to ‘repeats.’
You have reduced a supernatural exclusive to a plumbing complaint.
Now people can fix it.
A dangerous precedent for a newspaper.
The signal comes first. The clerk's line turns. Then the waiting launch moves.
So our reliable claim is that somebody was prepared.
Yes. Not that the sea joined the company.
I will reluctantly withdraw its employee portrait.
Don't sit down. The table has not approved the chairs.
Are the chairs applying separately?
That is precisely the sort of question this house encourages.
I'm following a signal relay with your family's name on it.
Then you have found a second system I would prefer to discuss while it is not boiling.
Warm tea. Parked table. Bell waiting for a person. Astonishingly ordinary.
You have removed the management structure.
It was obstructing the door.
Come into the workshop.
The house is working. Are we allowed to sit?
The chairs have formed a waiting list.
At least they've found a standing arrangement.
What does it make of pocket lint?
An unlicensed nebula. Please keep it. The sorter charges by constellation.
My family made local routing gear. Gates, relays, things that should be boring when they work.
The company signals before the current turns.
Then someone has put part of the network back into service.
Can it control the tide?
It can redirect water through connected channels. The moon remains regrettably independent.
A striped cabin behind a movable wall. Either Orin's ship is here, or architecture has taken up sailing.
Second Opinion. Present, afloat, and making a strong case against ‘vanished.’
I followed the new marker. It led straight into the service inlet.
And when the barrier closed?
I called it fog. I was standing on land at the time.
The marker was wrong for your journey. You can say that without claiming the ship evaporated.
I trusted the sign over what I knew. There. An unpleasantly navigable sentence.
Can she reach Bellweather Shoal?
With a current survey and someone willing to question the navigator.
I have been practising.
The drain and pillar agree with the old drawing. The basin gives me the missing level.
A short service channel. A small correction. I can finally put my name beside something useful.
Second Opinion. Cream cabin, three blue stripes, copper kettle for a weather vane.
A kettle?
It always points away from the weather. Better judgement than several instruments.
Where did you last see her?
By the new arrow behind the repair yards. I stepped ashore. When I returned, a timber screen occupied the view.
You have a boat and a correction. An unusually productive afternoon.
The boat was already there. That was part of the correction.
And the service measurement?
Checked against fixed marks, with the basin equalised.
Then let us put your name on it.
Original retained. Working copy dated. Uncertainty labelled instead of wished away.
Here is the copy. The correction is local. The limitations are on the page.
And your name is on the commission. Twelve crowns, credited in full.
Independent surveyor Nell.
You have made the missing connection.
I hope it helps people find their way.
It will make the route dependable.
At the next major tide, all commercial passage through the managed channels will operate under a Fair Passage contract.
All passage?
Uncoordinated access makes coordinated safety impossible.
You hired me to correct a route.
And you did. Excellently.
That's my correction. Not a forgery. Not a misunderstanding.
I helped finish the route they mean to charge everyone for.
I wanted somebody important to say my work mattered.
It matters. Now I have to decide what I do about that.
Right, Nell. Take stock. You have a borrowed boathook, an old survey, and a pencil that has somehow become responsible for your career.
At the landing, the signal came first. Then the local current changed. Then the company launch sailed through. That is a sequence, not proof that somebody has bought the ocean.
I need other witnesses. Pip’s newspaper might have reports worth comparing, once I separate the facts from the exciting punctuation.
Then there is the signal hardware at the repair quay. Find its maker, find out what it actually does. Preferably before touching anything labelled experimental.
And Orin’s missing ship. Boats rarely disappear out of embarrassment, even when their navigators would like them to. I should ask him for a proper description.
Check the witnesses. Follow the machinery. Find the boat. If I can explain this harbour, perhaps I can finally reach Bellweather Shoal. One well-supported mistake at a time.
I was told you understand the harbour machinery.
The credit is real. So is what they have done with the measurements.
I will meet you at the inlet. Bring a proper mooring line.
I need their attention, not their coat.
A poor conversationalist. Excellent at holding its position.
You may look. I am keeping the original.
A rope with a purpose. This puts it ahead of several committees.
The mooring rope is already doing its job at the inlet.
Observe what moves. Then observe what does not.
Got it. The small line can carry the big idea.
A little farther than an arm. Fortunately, I borrowed a longer argument.
A sound line to a sound post. Refreshingly little philosophy.
The basin is calm. The staff reads the middle marked line.
Let the two levels settle first.
Useful here. Awkward in a pocket.
I have enough. An expedition need not begin with hoarding.
One sheet. I intend to make a small, precise mess.
Different witnesses. The same order. Enough to investigate; not enough to accuse everyone with a bell.
T. ROOK & FAMILY. LOCAL CHANNEL RELAY 7. TOWN LANE WORKSHOP. A clue with excellent manners.
Witness statements. The useful bits have survived the handwriting.
Courtesy paper. A rare form of paper that does not want something.
Public mooring line. Return it attached to something that ought to stay put.
A firm surface for making a careful copy.
Public inspection access must remain operable during trials.
A company route sheet, carrying my service-channel annotation.
Ink on one cuff. More ink on the cuff used to wipe it off.
Each pigeonhole contains evidence. The pigeons appear to have escaped questioning.
A place to check a sentence before it becomes everybody’s problem.
One clean sheet amid a forest of accusations.
LIGHTHOUSE PREDICTS YESTERDAY. At least it can check its work.
A machine for making a small error very widely available.
An inventor trying to prevent tea from entering a new state of matter.
The heater waits for the bell. The bell waits for the table. The table waits for the heater.
PARK HERE BEFORE RELEASING TROLLEY. The furniture is better instructed than most crews.
RESERVED FOR OCCUPANT. OCCUPANT AWAITING RESERVATION.
It has classified a potato peel as a minor moon.
She reads the little words before touching the big levers.
Three channels, linked gates, one basin. A sea small enough to contradict politely.
SERVICE INLET 7. Fixed marks: square drain; split granite pillar.
Square socket. Long handle. A respectable way to disagree with a gate.
Several generations looking certain about progressively larger machines.
Cream cabin. Three blue stripes. A copper kettle where the weather vane should be.
RUN or INSPECT. I would like the setting that expects questions.
The thin line brings the heavy rope aboard. A small job with a sensible ambition.
Sound timber. No theatrical opinions about ownership.
Square drain, at the waterline. A fixed mark that does not mind getting wet.
That crack appears on the old drawing. Stone has been keeping notes.
Three clearly marked levels. I need the equalised reading.
Align the square drain and the split granite pillar.
Three stripes, copper kettle, and an owner who owes it an apology.
His certainty is quieter near the boat.
Composed, attentive, and very certain where every page belongs.
Provisional local routing trials. Public inspection access must remain available.
The harbour, reduced to something one person can put a hand over.
Twelve crowns for a verified annotated copy. Operational calibration and local route planning. The original remains mine.
For copies. My original is remaining unusually close to me.
CENTRAL EMERGENCY SIGNALS TO BE ANNOUNCED PUBLICLY.
Practical advice, without a charge for the truth.
A navigator whose vessel is still waiting for him.
Empty, with the key still in its lock. My original survey stays with me.
An old rival trying to remain relevant.
A partner, not a talking accessory.
The float remains safely tethered. The signal preceded the change.
My baseline and the observation are preserved in the notebook.

Eccentric brass clockwork dining room, quiet clock ticking, faint tea steam and gentle pipe rattles. No voices or music. Seamless loop.
Quiet nautical inventors workshop, subdued small gears and clockwork, occasional soft metal tick, warm room tone. No voices, no music. Seamless loop.
Sheltered old harbour inlet, gentle water lapping stone and wooden boat hulls, distant breeze, subtle rope creaking. No voices or music. Seamless loop.
Quiet elegant wooden harbourside office, muted water outside, gentle wall clock and occasional paper rustle. No voices or music. Seamless loop.
Heavy but safe old brass and iron mechanism turning, followed by a clear solid latch click. No voices or music.
Small sluice valve opens, water gently flows and settles in a harbour basin, controlled not violent. No speech or music.
A wooden office stamp firmly stamps parchment on a leather desk pad, then paper slides. No voices or music.
